title: Other people's data: what you can put in and what you can't
promise: You'll be able to decide, document by document, what can go into an AI tool and what can't, and you'll set up the step beforehand that strips out what isn't needed. By the end you'll have your data sorted and a written rule you could show if you were asked for it.
why: Nuria was about to upload her practice's entire folder to a Project, payroll included. She was stopped by a question from a colleague: «and if a client asks you where their data is?». She had no answer. She didn't know which country the servers were in, whether it was used for training, or what she'd say to a client who asked. It wasn't that she was doing anything illegal: it was that she was about to do it without being able to explain it, and that's where the real trouble starts.

theory.title: The question that settles 90% of cases
theory.text: You don't need to be a lawyer to get almost all of these decisions right. There's one question that works as a filter and it's this: if the contents of this document appeared on the internet tomorrow, would I have a serious problem with the person named inside it? If the answer is yes, that document doesn't go into an AI tool until you've thought through the rest of this lesson. If it's no, in it goes without fuss. It isn't a legal rule, it's a practical one, and it filters well because what you're measuring is exactly what matters: harm to a third party who has decided nothing about any of this.
theory.analogy: It's the same question you ask yourself before forwarding an email to someone else. You don't consult the regulations: you think about whether whoever wrote it would be happy about it.
theory.example: A blank template contract with no names: goes in. An employee's payslip with her ID number, her account and a garnishment: doesn't.

theory.title: The three piles
theory.text: Everything you have fits into three piles and sorting it takes less than you'd think. The first: anything with nobody's data in it. Templates, your own criteria, regulations, technical documentation, blank template contracts. In it goes without thinking. The second: anything with ordinary personal data. Names, phone numbers, emails, addresses. It can go in, but with conditions, and those conditions are what you'll see in the rest of the lesson. And the third, the one that stays out: the delicate material. Two different things live there and it's worth not confusing them. On one hand, what European law calls special categories: health, ethnic origin, political opinions, religious beliefs, trade union membership, sex life or sexual orientation, and genetic or biometric data. On the other, things that aren't a special category but equally have no business going in: criminal records, which have their own separate footing; data about minors, which carries reinforced protection; and banking data, which is ordinary in legal terms and an enormous problem in practice if it leaks. For today's decision it doesn't matter which drawer each falls into: neither group goes in without specific advice. Most people discover while sorting that the first pile is far bigger than they thought, and that it alone covers nearly everything they wanted to do.
theory.example: Nuria: 192 documents. 140 into the first pile, 38 into the second and 14 into the third. With those 140 she already had 90% of her queries covered.

theory.title: Stripping out what isn't needed before uploading
theory.text: For the second pile there's a very good and rarely used way out: taking the personal data out before putting them in. You almost never need it. If your question is «what terms did I agree in this contract?», the client's name adds nothing to the answer. You replace it with CLIENT-1 and it works exactly the same. Likewise with phone numbers, ID numbers, addresses and accounts. And if you need to know whose it was, you keep a separate table saying CLIENT-1 is Ferretería Beltrán, on your computer and not uploaded anywhere. With that, the document moves from the second pile to the first and the problem disappears.
theory.example: «Contract with Ferretería Beltrán, tax ID B12345678, automatic annual renewal» → «Contract with CLIENT-1, automatic annual renewal». The answer to your question is identical.

theory.title: The three things to check about any tool
theory.text: Before putting people's data into any tool you have to check three things, and all three are on its website even if they take finding. One: whether they use what you upload to train their models, and whether that can be switched off. On business plans it usually ships switched off; on personal ones, sometimes not. Two: where the servers are, because if European data is involved it matters. And three: whether they offer a data processing agreement, which is the paperwork you need if you handle clients' data. That such a document exists is also the best sign the tool is built for professional use. Write the three answers down with the date, because they change and because the day someone asks you'll want to show something more than a recollection.
theory.example: Nuria checked and noted: «Claude, Team plan, doesn't train on business data, servers in the US with European clauses, processing agreement signed on 3 September.» Four lines, and the conversation with a client stops being frightening.

theory.title: What students usually get wrong without noticing
theory.text: There are three slips that repeat and none of them looks serious at the time. First: pasting a whole email into a chat to get help drafting a reply, with the signature, the phone number and the client's case inside it. Second: taking a screenshot for a tutorial or to ask a question, with the client list visible in the background. And third: testing a new setup «with real data to see whether it works», when testing with invented data would have given exactly the same information. That third is the commonest of all and the easiest to avoid: to test, invent the data.
theory.example: «Help me answer this email» plus the whole email pasted in with the sender, their phone number and their case. The help would have been the same with those three details removed.

theory.title: Being able to explain it is worth more than getting it right by luck
theory.text: The difference between someone who works well with this and someone heading for trouble isn't what they do, it's whether they can explain it. If a client asks where their data is and what tools you use, the answer can't be «I don't know». With half a page written — which tools you use, what kind of data goes into each, what you strip before uploading and what you've checked about each provider — that conversation is settled. And that half page is also what you'll be asked for if you do this for a company or if you present your final project.
theory.example: Nuria has a sheet titled «Which tools I use and with what data». When a client asks, she shows it. She has never had to give further explanations.

tasks.title: Sort your documents into the three piles
tasks.where: In your clean folder from block 07, or your project's folder
tasks.action: Create three subfolders: «no-data», «ordinary-data» and «sensitive-data». Move each document into whichever it belongs to, using the filter question. Don't agonise over each one: if you're torn between two piles, put it in the more restrictive one and move on. The hesitation itself is information.
tasks.expect: Three folders with an uneven split: «no-data» is normally the biggest by far. Note how many are in each.
tasks.stuck: If nearly everything lands in «ordinary-data», check whether you genuinely need the names for what you're going to ask. Almost always you don't, and then task 3 moves them into the first pile.

tasks.title: Check the three things about your tool
tasks.action: Find on their site the answers to the three questions: whether they use what you upload for training and how it's switched off, where the servers are, and whether they offer a data processing agreement. It's usually on the privacy, trust or security pages. Write the three answers with today's date in a file called «tools-and-data.txt».
tasks.expect: Three answers written with a date. If you can't find one, write «not found» and the date: that's information too, and in some cases it's reason enough not to put client data there.
tasks.stuck: If you get lost in the legal text, paste the link or the text into a chat with the AI and ask for exactly those three answers, with the document's literal sentence saying so. Here it's worth asking for the verbatim, so you can quote it.

tasks.title: Set up the data stripping
tasks.where: On the documents in the «ordinary-data» pile
tasks.action: Take five documents from that pile and replace the personal data with labels: CLIENT-1, PHONE-1, ID-1. Keep it consistent: the same client always with the same number. Separately, in a file that stays on your computer and isn't uploaded anywhere, write the lookup table.
tasks.expect: Five documents with no personal data inside and a lookup table saved separately. Try asking one of them a question: you'll see the answer you needed is exactly the same.
tasks.stuck: If there are many documents, run this test before committing: take one, strip its data, and check whether the answer you were after still comes out. If it does, the work is worth it. If it turns out you did need the names, then it's a different decision and the route is a contract with the provider.

tasks.title: Have the AI review a document before you upload it
tasks.action: Before uploading a batch, give it one sample and ask it to point out what's inside. Mind the irony of this task: use it with a document from the «no-data» pile or one already anonymised, not with a sensitive one.
tasks.prompt:
I'm giving you a document from my work. I want to know what information about people it contains before deciding whether to upload it to an AI tool.

TELL ME, as a list and nothing else:
1. What personal data appears and on which line or section: names, surnames, ID numbers, phone numbers, emails, addresses, bank accounts, vehicle registrations, case numbers.
2. Whether anything delicate appears, in two separate lists: (a) GDPR special categories: health, ethnic origin, political opinions, beliefs, trade union membership, sex life or sexual orientation, genetic or biometric data; (b) other data that also shouldn't be uploaded: criminal records, data about minors and banking data.
3. For each item in list 1: whether it's needed in order to answer questions about the document's content, or whether it can be replaced by a label without losing anything.

Don't give me legal advice or opinions. Just the three lists.

DOCUMENT:
[PASTE HERE]
tasks.expect: A list of what's inside and, above all, the third column: almost everything can be replaced. That's what turns a second-pile document into a first-pile one.
tasks.stuck: If it answers with generic legal recommendations, cut it short: «I don't want recommendations. Tell me which specific data appear and on which line.»

tasks.title: Always test with invented data
tasks.action: Take your five test cases from lesson 35 and check whether any of them contains real people's data. If so, swap them for invented ones that look similar in shape: same number of digits in the phone number, surnames just as awkward, addresses just as long. The shape is what makes a test case useful; whether the person exists adds nothing.
tasks.expect: Five test cases without a single real person in them. From now on you test without having to think about this.
tasks.stuck: If you need data that closely resembles the real thing, ask the AI to generate twenty fake records in your country's format: compound names, hyphenated surnames, phone numbers with the right prefix. They serve just as well and they belong to nobody.

tasks.title: Write your half page
tasks.action: Write, so you can show it: which tools you use, what kind of data goes into each (using the three piles), what you strip before uploading, what you checked about each provider and when, and what you never put in. Date it and set yourself a reminder to review it every six months.
tasks.expect: Half a page. This is the answer to «where is my data?» and to the equivalent question at your final project's defence.
tasks.stuck: If while writing it you realise there's something you couldn't defend in front of a client, that isn't a problem with the document: it's that that something shouldn't be uploaded. Take it out and then write.

matters: That the filter question is whether the document going public would harm whoever is named inside it.
That specially protected data doesn't go in, and that includes health, genetic and biometric data.
That criminal records, minors' data and banking data aren't special categories, and equally don't go in.
That being able to explain what you do is worth more than having got it right without knowing.
ignore: Memorising the regulation's articles. The filter question and the three piles settle nearly everything.
The arguments about whether AIs respect privacy. What decides is what you upload.
Hunting for the perfect tool. What matters is what you put into the one you use.
canDo: Sort any document into one of the three piles in seconds.
Turn a document with personal data into one you can upload.
Know whether your tool trains on what you upload and where the servers are.
Answer a client in writing when they ask where their data is.
cantDo: Replace legal advice if you handle sensitive data at volume.
Get back what you already uploaded to somewhere that trains on it.
Put health, banking or minors' data in under these rules.
Know what the provider will do in two years: that's why you date it and review.
words: Anything that identifies a person: name, phone number, email, ID number, registration.

The kinds of data European law protects most strongly: health, ethnic origin, political opinions, beliefs, trade union membership, sex life or sexual orientation, genetic or biometric data. They don't go in.
Delicate data that isn't a special category
Criminal records, minors' data and banking data. Legally they run on a different footing, but they equally don't go into an AI tool without thought.
Replacing personal data with labels, keeping the lookup separately and not uploading it.
The contract with the provider that lets you put your clients' data into their tool.
The provider using what you upload to improve their models. It can usually be switched off.
